A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ACE framework and retain matching core experiments. Text extraction and visual inspection cover all 23 pages of v2 and 32 pages of v3, including figures, tables and appendices, without material reading gaps.

before.justification: v2 reports original AppWorld, FiNER and Formula experiments, component ablations, and adaptation cost and latency measurements in Tables 1–4.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds experiments across models and domains, robustness tests, sensitivity analyses and detailed cost measurements in Appendix A.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the Generator–Reflector–Curator workflow, itemized context bullets, deterministic delta merging and grow-and-refine mechanism. The prompt contents in Figures 6–14 match across versions. Additional model configurations and ablations evaluate the existing procedure; no algorithm revision is established.

E1.justification: v3 retains AppWorld, FiNER and Formula and adds offline evaluation on StreamBench's DDXPlus medical diagnosis and BIRD-SQL text-to-SQL tasks (Section 4.1 and Appendix A.2). These introduce substantially different domains and task requirements beyond the original agent and finance coverage.

E2.justification: The original accuracy comparisons retain their baseline membership. The new evaluation-stage cost comparisons include Base ReAct alongside GEPA and ACE (Tables 14–15), extending v2's cost comparisons against GEPA and DC in Table 4. Added accuracy studies reuse existing comparison methods.

E3.justification: v3 adds GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.1 and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct configurations. New domain evaluations use 1,000 training examples, specified GEPA validation sets, and GPT-4o-mini judging for BIRD-SQL. Appendix A also introduces controlled reflector and hyperparameter variations and a cost study using one epoch and one reflection round. These are additional protocols; the original main-experiment settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained Reflector, multi-epoch and warmup ablations, v3 tests removal of incremental updates, varying Reflector capability, adversarial feedback frequency, reflection rounds, deduplication thresholds and pruning triggers (Appendices A.4–A.6). It also adds component-level adaptation/evaluation cost analyses and measured prompt-cache reuse, addressing previously untested mechanisms and tradeoffs.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeat counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added tables continue reporting point estimates; their signed differences indicate changes relative to baselines, not uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their numerical results, while Tables 5–21 add substantial new findings. For example, DDXPlus accuracy is 90.2 for ACE versus 75.2 for the base model and 76.4 for GEPA. BIRD-SQL averages are 52.9, 47.8 and 52.2 respectively, with GEPA ahead on Moderate and Challenging subsets. Further additions quantify model-dependent gains, robustness, ablation effects and token costs.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theorems or proofs. The procedural account of ACE is retained, and the new appendices add empirical analyses and conceptual discussion without new mathematical definitions or derivations.

C1.justification: The central ACE contributions and headline gains of 10.6% on agents and 8.6% on finance remain. However, the introduction changes from matching IBM-CUGA overall and surpassing it on test-challenge to an unqualified claim of surpassing the top-ranked agent. The original scores and narrower abstract/Section 4.3 account remain, making this a limited strengthening of the leaderboard claim.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of transfer across model families, tolerance to weak and corrupted reflections, excessive reflection, pruning tradeoffs, and raw versus cache-discounted token costs (Sections 4.5–4.7 and Appendix A). A new Section 4.3 footnote qualifies CUGA as a contextual reference. The original limitations are retained in Section 5, alongside these expanded applicability and mechanism discussions.

D1.justification: v3 documents additional experiment-specific sample sizes, model assignments, adaptation budgets, corruption frequencies, threshold ranges and use of GPT-5.1's default prompt caching. These extend the technical record, while the existing role prompts and code-access destination remain unchanged. The new reproducibility statement mainly consolidates existing disclosures.

R1.justification: v3 adds references supporting the new benchmarks, judging procedure, caching discussion and robustness discussion, and Appendix C expands comparisons with GEPA and Dynamic Cheatsheet. Explicit acknowledgment of building on Dynamic Cheatsheet is removed from the abstract and introduction, although Section 3 retains the connection. The broader positioning around context adaptation remains stable.

P1.justification: The main narrative sequence and most existing method and prompt language are retained. v3 makes localized rewrites, adds explanatory subsections and conference statements, moves limitations into Section 5, and integrates the previous caching discussion into cost analysis. Citations switch to author–year formatting, and the appendices are reorganized around extended results and discussions.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 5–21 covering model comparisons, new domains, cost breakdowns and sensitivity tests. It also adopts the ICLR layout, resizes and relocates existing displays, and changes Figure 1's axis ranges and tick spacing. The original figures, including the leaderboard snapshot and prompt displays, are retained.

improvement.justification: The direct incremental-update ablation and reflection stress tests address important gaps in v2's evidence for ACE's mechanism and failure conditions. Additional model and domain evaluations substantially strengthen generalizability, while measured caching and token breakdowns clarify serving-cost tradeoffs. These gains outweigh localized overclaims, including the strengthened CUGA statement and Appendix A.1's assertion that online adaptation is consistently strongest, which Tables 7–9 do not support. Statistical uncertainty remains unreported.
